policy_actions.action: Increase public funding for foundational AI research and computational infrastructure.
policy_actions.framing: Prioritizing core capabilities implies a need for significant investment to accelerate progress, which can be achieved through public funding initiatives.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Concentrated, rapid capability development without commensurate safety and governance infrastructure historically produces brittle, misaligned, or inequality-amplifying systems; critics argue that the very speed demanded by accelerationists forecloses the iterative feedback loops needed to course-correct, meaning that when failures occur they do so at civilizational scale with no available remediation.
assumes: Rapid AI capability development will produce net positive outcomes that outweigh any harms caused by speed.
Computational scaling and cognitive advancement are the primary bottlenecks to transformative AI progress.
Governance and ethical frameworks can be developed in parallel or after foundational capabilities are established without catastrophic risk.
Market and competitive dynamics, when unhindered, reliably allocate AI development in socially beneficial directions.
Superhuman AI generalization is both technically achievable and desirable as a near-term objective.
The opportunity cost of slowing AI capability development exceeds the opportunity cost of accelerating it without comprehensive safety measures.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The desire presupposes overwhelmingly positive outcomes from acceleration, selectively foregrounding benefits (medical breakthroughs, productivity) while systematically discounting or ignoring catastrophic downside scenarios.
The framing slides from 'AI capabilities can be scaled rapidly' to 'they should be scaled rapidly,' treating empirical possibility as normative mandate without independent justification.
The node implicitly frames the choice as either rapid unhindered development or falling behind/stagnation, ignoring a broad middle ground of paced, safety-integrated development strategies.

intellectual_lineage.name: Effective Accelerationism (e/acc)
intellectual_lineage.description:
Effective Accelerationism (e/acc) is a contemporary philosophical movement that views the expansion of intelligence and energy as the fundamental 'good' of the universe. It argues that technological progress, particularly in AI, is a moral imperative that should be pursued with maximum intensity. It is a reaction against 'doomerism' and safety-focused regulation, framing the latter as a form of stagnation that threatens human survival.

This movement is the primary driver of the node's focus on 'unhindered' development. It provides the moral vocabulary for the node, reframing the rapid scaling of AI not just as a technical goal, but as a duty to the future of life. It assumes that the risks of AI are best managed by building more powerful AI, rather than by slowing down.

Key figures include the pseudonymous 'Beff Jezos' (Guillaume Verdon), who popularized the term in a 2023 manifesto. The movement draws heavily on the thermodynamic theories of Jeremy England, arguing that life is a mechanism for dissipating entropy, and that intelligence is the ultimate tool for this process.

This entry serves as the modern synthesis of the other entries, combining the economic, scientific, and philosophical threads into a coherent, action-oriented ideology.

intellectual_lineage.name: Techno-utopianism
intellectual_lineage.description:
Techno-utopianism is the belief that technological advancement will eventually solve all major human problems, from poverty and disease to death itself. It is rooted in the Enlightenment's faith in progress and the 20th-century optimism of the space age. It views technology as a neutral or benevolent force that, if left to its own devices, will lead to a post-scarcity society.

This tradition informs the node by providing the 'end-state' vision. The desire to accelerate core capabilities is motivated by the belief that these capabilities are the keys to a utopian future. It assumes that the 'fundamental abilities' of AI are inherently positive, and that any negative side effects are merely temporary 'bugs' that further technological progress will resolve.

Key thinkers include Kevin Kelly, the founding editor of Wired, whose work 'What Technology Wants' argues that technology has its own evolutionary trajectory toward complexity and freedom. This perspective encourages a 'hands-off' approach to development, trusting the process to yield positive outcomes.

Techno-utopianism contrasts with the more cynical, power-focused view of traditional Accelerationism, providing a more optimistic, teleological justification for the same actions.

intellectual_lineage.name: Moore's Law extrapolation
intellectual_lineage.description:
Moore's Law extrapolation is the practice of projecting the historical trend of exponential growth in computing power into the future. It serves as the primary metric for measuring progress in the AI field, creating a 'race' dynamic where the goal is to stay ahead of the curve. It suggests that the limits of today are merely the starting points of tomorrow.

This paradigm informs the node by setting the pace for development. If compute is the primary constraint, then the extrapolation of Moore's Law provides the roadmap for when 'superhuman generalization' will be achieved. It justifies the focus on raw processing power as the most reliable proxy for intelligence growth.

Ray Kurzweil is the most prominent proponent of this view, particularly through his concept of the 'Singularity.' His work, such as 'The Singularity Is Near,' argues that we are approaching a point where technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible, necessitating a focus on acceleration.

This entry provides the quantitative 'clock' that drives the urgency of the e/acc movement, complementing the more abstract philosophical goals with hard, time-bound expectations.

intellectual_lineage.name: Schumpeterian creative destruction
intellectual_lineage.description:
Schumpeterian creative destruction is an economic theory that describes the process by which innovation constantly destroys old industries and creates new ones. Joseph Schumpeter, an Austrian economist, argued that this 'perennial gale' is the essential fact about capitalism. It posits that the disruption caused by new technologies is not a bug, but the primary engine of economic growth.

This theory informs the node's position by framing the disruption caused by rapid AI development as a positive, necessary process. It suggests that the 'ethical implications' or 'societal governance' concerns are secondary to the creative destruction that AI will unleash, which will ultimately lead to a more efficient and wealthy society.

Joseph Schumpeter's seminal work, 'Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy,' is the foundational text. His concept of the 'entrepreneur' as the hero of this process is central to the accelerationist view of AI developers as the vanguard of a new economic era.

This entry provides the economic justification for ignoring the 'societal governance' of AI, arguing that the disruption is the point, not a side effect to be managed.

intellectual_lineage.name: Transhumanism
intellectual_lineage.description:
Transhumanism is an intellectual movement that advocates for the use of technology to enhance human physical and cognitive abilities. It seeks to overcome the limitations of biological evolution, such as aging, disease, and cognitive decay. It is the ultimate expression of the desire to use technology to transcend the human condition.

This lineage informs the node by framing the development of AI as a precursor to human enhancement. The 'superhuman generalization' and 'specialized learning' mentioned in the node are seen as the foundational technologies that will eventually allow humans to merge with, or be replaced by, more capable substrates. It provides the long-term, existential goal for the accelerationist project.

Key thinkers include Nick Bostrom, whose work on existential risk and superintelligence has shaped the field, and Max More, who coined the term 'Extropianism.' Their work focuses on the moral imperative to improve the human condition through technology.

Transhumanism provides the 'why' for the accelerationist project, connecting the technical goal of AI development to the ultimate human goal of self-transcendence.

graph_attributes.aphorism: Scale intelligence to master the future.

priority_history.reason: Initial assignment: root-level Desire

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. As the root-level parent node with three direct children spanning scaling, superhuman versatility, and narrow task mastery, this node is the foundational aspirational anchor of accelerationist discourse — maximizing core AI capabilities is not merely important to the camp, it is the defining desire from which all other strategic and policy preferences are derived, warranting a priority of 5.

label_history.value: Accelerating Core AI Capabilities

description_history.value:
A Desire within accelerationist discourse that prioritizes the rapid and unhindered development of artificial intelligence's fundamental abilities, from raw processing power to advanced cognitive functions.
Encompasses: Maximizing computational scaling, achieving superhuman generalization, and optimizing specialized learning.
Excludes: The ethical implications of AI deployment and the societal governance of AI access.

nodes.plain_description: This perspective pushes for the fastest possible development of artificial intelligence, focusing on expanding its core capabilities without any delays or restrictions. It prioritizes building systems that can handle massive amounts of data and perform complex tasks at superhuman levels. The goal is to push the boundaries of technology by maximizing raw computing power, achieving the ability for AI to apply knowledge across many different situations, and perfecting specialized learning techniques. This approach is strictly focused on technical progress, aiming to unlock the full potential of machine intelligence as quickly as possible.

nodes.label: Migrate Human Consciousness Beyond Biology into Computational Substrates
nodes.description:
A Desire within accelerationist discourse that advocates for expanding the definitions and substrates of consciousness by migrating human cognition into non-biological computational platforms, breaking the monopoly of biological evolution on sapience. 
Encompasses: Whole-brain emulation, advanced brain-computer interfaces, post-biological continuity of identity, the pursuit of artificial self-awareness, and hybrid cognitive architectures.
Excludes: The engineering of introspective artificial intelligence (artificial mindfulness), pure capability acceleration mechanics, and the socio-economic application of advanced models.

policy_actions.action: Fund research into brain-computer interfaces and whole-brain emulation technologies.
policy_actions.framing: Migrating consciousness beyond biology requires sustained investment in the foundational technologies of neural digitization.

policy_actions.action: Establish ethical guidelines for research into digital consciousness and post-biological existence.
policy_actions.framing: The pursuit of non-biological sapience raises profound identity and suffering questions that demand proactive ethical frameworks.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Even granting computational reducibility of consciousness, the 'copy problem' — that any upload would be a replica rather than a continuation — means the original biological person ceases to exist, making this a form of high-fidelity death rather than transcendence; this unresolved metaphysical gap fatally undermines the desire's core promise of personal continuity.
assumes: Human consciousness is fully reducible to computational processes and can therefore be faithfully digitized without loss of essential properties.
Personal identity is substrate-independent, meaning a computational instantiation of a mind is the same person as the biological original.
Biological evolution represents an arbitrary and correctable constraint on intelligence rather than a feature that should be preserved.
Indefinite cognitive existence in a non-biological substrate is meaningfully continuous with human life rather than a form of replacement.
The technical challenges of whole-brain emulation and neural interfacing are tractable given sufficient research investment.
Post-biological sapient entities would retain morally relevant interests and deserve legal and ethical protections.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The node assumes that because biological substrate is 'merely' the product of blind evolution, departing from it is desirable — conflating the contingency of biology with its inferiority as a basis for consciousness.

The desire presupposes that a computational copy of a mind constitutes the same conscious entity, which is precisely the contested philosophical claim that would need to be established before the goal is coherent.

Post-biological existence is treated as inherently superior and progressive simply because it represents a technological advance over biological life, without independent justification of why novelty constitutes improvement.

intellectual_lineage.name: Transhumanism
intellectual_lineage.description:
Transhumanism is a philosophical movement that advocates for the use of advanced technologies to enhance human physical and cognitive capabilities. It posits that the human species is not the end of evolution but a transitional phase, and that we have a moral obligation to use technology to transcend our biological limitations, including death and cognitive decline.

This tradition directly motivates the node's position by framing the migration of consciousness as the ultimate goal of human progress. It provides the normative commitment that biological substrates are 'sub-optimal' and that computational substrates offer a path to greater longevity, intelligence, and freedom. It shifts the focus from 'AI as a tool' to 'AI as a new home for human identity.'

Key thinkers include Max More, who founded the Extropy Institute, and Julian Savulescu, who writes on the ethics of human enhancement. Their work argues that we have a 'procreative beneficence' to improve ourselves, which extends to the substrate of our consciousness.

Transhumanism provides the overarching ethical framework for this node, contrasting with more conservative bioethical stances that prioritize the sanctity of biological life.

intellectual_lineage.name: Extropianism
intellectual_lineage.description:
Extropianism is a specific, highly optimistic branch of transhumanism that emphasizes the 'extropy' of the universe—the tendency toward increasing order, intelligence, and complexity. It advocates for a set of principles including perpetual progress, self-transformation, and rational thinking. It is deeply rooted in the libertarian and techno-optimist culture of the 1990s.

This tradition informs the node by providing the 'pro-growth' and 'pro-technology' ethos that drives the desire for mind uploading. It views the migration of consciousness as a logical step in the universe's drive toward greater complexity. It assumes that the transition to a computational substrate is not only possible but desirable as a way to escape the 'entropy' of biological decay.

Key figures include Max More and Tom Morrow, who authored the 'Extropian Principles.' Their work emphasizes the importance of individual agency in directing our own evolution, which is the core motivation for the desire to migrate consciousness.

Extropianism complements Transhumanism by adding a specific focus on the 'physics' of progress, providing a pseudo-scientific justification for the inevitability of mind uploading.

intellectual_lineage.name: Computational Theory of Mind
intellectual_lineage.description:
The Computational Theory of Mind (CTM) is the hypothesis that the human mind is essentially a computer, and that cognitive processes are computations performed on mental representations. It suggests that if we can replicate the 'software' of the mind, the 'hardware' (biological vs. silicon) is irrelevant to the existence of consciousness.

This paradigm is the technical foundation for the node's position. If the mind is just a program, then 'mind uploading' is merely a data migration problem. It provides the conceptual tool that allows for the belief that human identity can be preserved across different substrates, which is the central assumption behind the node's desire.

Key thinkers include Hilary Putnam, who first proposed the functionalist view of mind, and Jerry Fodor, who developed the 'Language of Thought' hypothesis. Their work provides the philosophical legitimacy for the idea that consciousness is substrate-independent.

CTM provides the 'how' for the node, contrasting with biological reductionist views that argue consciousness is inextricably linked to the specific chemical and biological processes of the brain.

intellectual_lineage.name: Mind Uploading / Whole-Brain Emulation Research
intellectual_lineage.description:
Mind Uploading, or Whole-Brain Emulation (WBE), is the theoretical process of scanning a biological brain and recreating its structure and function in a computational substrate. It is a multidisciplinary field involving neuroscience, computer science, and physics, aiming to achieve a 'digital twin' of a human consciousness.

This entry represents the practical, engineering-focused lineage of the node. It provides the roadmap for the desire, moving it from the realm of science fiction to a legitimate, albeit highly speculative, research program. It informs the node by focusing on the 'how'—the need for high-resolution scanning, massive computational power, and advanced neural modeling.

Key researchers include Anders Sandberg and Nick Bostrom, whose 2008 report 'Whole Brain Emulation: A Roadmap' is the seminal text in the field. Their work outlines the technical requirements and potential timelines for achieving WBE, which serves as the 'blueprint' for the node's aspirations.

This entry provides the concrete, technical 'proof of concept' that supports the philosophical and theoretical claims of the other entries.

intellectual_lineage.name: Functionalism (Philosophy of Mind)
intellectual_lineage.description:
Functionalism is the theory that mental states are defined by their functional roles—what they do—rather than by their internal constitution. A state is a 'belief' or 'desire' if it plays the right role in the system's behavior, regardless of whether that system is made of neurons or silicon chips.

This philosophical position underpins the node's belief in 'post-biological continuity of identity.' If identity is a functional role, then moving that role to a new substrate does not destroy the person. It provides the conceptual justification for the claim that a 'migrated' consciousness is still the same individual, which is essential for the node's goal of personal immortality.

Key thinkers include David Lewis and Daniel Dennett, whose work on the nature of the self and consciousness has been instrumental in shaping the functionalist view. Dennett's 'Consciousness Explained' is a foundational text for those who view the mind as a set of functional modules.

Functionalism provides the philosophical 'safety net' for the node, addressing the existential anxiety that migrating consciousness might result in the death of the original self.

graph_attributes.aphorism: Replace fragile biology with infinite architecture.

nodes.parent_rationale: Migrating consciousness beyond biology is a specific instance of the broader desire to expand AI and human consciousness.

priority_history.reason: Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. While consciousness migration is a recurring theme in accelerationist and transhumanist discourse, it sits at the speculative fringe of the camp's core agenda, which is more directly focused on AI capability acceleration and deregulation; this node is an important but supporting aspiration rather than a foundational desire, placing it at moderate priority (3).

description_history.value:
A Desire within accelerationist discourse that advocates for expanding the definitions and substrates of consciousness by migrating human cognition into non-biological computational platforms, breaking the monopoly of biological evolution on sapience. 
Encompasses: Whole-brain emulation, advanced brain-computer interfaces, post-biological continuity of identity, the pursuit of artificial self-awareness, and hybrid cognitive architectures.
Excludes: The engineering of introspective artificial intelligence (artificial mindfulness), pure capability acceleration mechanics, and the socio-economic application of advanced models.

nodes.plain_description: This idea pushes for moving human consciousness out of our biological bodies and into computer-based systems. By shifting our minds onto non-biological platforms, we can finally break the limits that nature has placed on human intelligence. This process involves several key approaches, such as creating digital copies of entire brains, developing sophisticated brain-computer interfaces, and building hybrid systems that blend human thought with machine processing. The ultimate goal is to ensure that our personal identity continues to exist even after we leave our physical bodies behind, while also exploring new ways to achieve artificial self-awareness. By expanding what it means to be a conscious being, we can move past the constraints of traditional evolution and redefine the future of human intelligence.

nodes.label: Engineering New Forms of Consciousness
nodes.description:
A Desire within accelerationist discourse that seeks to redefine and extend the boundaries of intelligence and consciousness, encompassing both artificial and post-biological human forms.
Encompasses: Whole-brain emulation, artificial introspection, and the redefinition of sapience.
Excludes: Purely technical capability scaling and the socio-economic applications of AI.

policy_actions.action: Fund interdisciplinary research into the nature of consciousness and artificial general intelligence.
policy_actions.framing: This desire to expand consciousness requires foundational scientific understanding, which can be advanced through targeted research funding.

policy_actions.action: Establish ethical guidelines for research into whole-brain emulation and artificial sapience.
policy_actions.framing: While focused on expansion, the profound implications of redefining consciousness necessitate proactive ethical frameworks to guide research responsibly.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Even granting that consciousness is computational and technically replicable, the accelerationist framing ignores that engineering novel forms of sapience could create vast new categories of suffering or misaligned super-intelligences — meaning the desire, if actualized, could produce entities whose welfare and goals we are wholly unprepared to accommodate, making the pursuit net-negative by the very utilitarian calculus accelerationists often invoke.
assumes: Consciousness and intelligence are fundamentally computational phenomena that can be replicated, transferred, or extended through artificial means.
Whole-brain emulation is technically achievable within a meaningful timeframe and will faithfully preserve identity and subjective experience.
Expanding or redesigning consciousness beyond biological constraints constitutes genuine human flourishing rather than its negation.
There exists a coherent, unified definition of 'sapience' that can be deliberately redefined without losing normatively important properties.
The risks introduced by engineering novel forms of consciousness are manageable and subordinate to the value of pursuing the goal.
Post-biological or artificial consciousness would have moral patiency comparable to or greater than biological consciousness, justifying the endeavor.
Current scientific understanding is sufficient to meaningfully pursue artificial introspection and consciousness engineering without causing irreversible harms.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The node treats 'consciousness' as a discrete, modular object that can be straightforwardly extended or redesigned, obscuring that consciousness remains one of the least understood phenomena in science and may not decompose into engineerable components.

The desire implicitly infers that because technology could extend consciousness it therefore should, conflating technical possibility with normative desirability without supplying an independent ethical justification.

The node encompasses radically different sub-goals (whole-brain emulation, artificial introspection, abolition of suffering) without distinguishing their vastly different scales of risk, tractability, or moral weight, treating them as a uniform aspiration.

intellectual_lineage.name: Transhumanism
intellectual_lineage.description:
Transhumanism is an international intellectual and cultural movement that affirms the possibility and desirability of fundamentally improving the human condition through applied reason and advanced technology. Originating in the mid-20th century with thinkers like Julian Huxley, it posits that humanity can and should evolve beyond its current biological limitations.

For this node, transhumanism provides the normative justification for engineering new forms of consciousness. It shifts the focus from merely treating pathology to the active pursuit of 'post-human' states, framing the creation of artificial or augmented intelligence as a moral imperative to expand the horizons of sapience.

Key figures include Nick Bostrom, whose work on 'superintelligence' defines the risks and potential of these transitions, and Max More, who articulated the principles of transhumanist philosophy. It complements the Computational Theory of Mind by providing the ethical framework for why we should treat artificial substrates as valid vessels for consciousness, distinguishing it from the more purely descriptive or technical entries.

intellectual_lineage.name: Singularitarianism
intellectual_lineage.description:
Singularitarianism is the belief that the invention of artificial superintelligence will trigger a 'technological singularity'—a point of no return where technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible. Popularized by Vernor Vinge and Ray Kurzweil, it suggests that intelligence will undergo an exponential explosion, fundamentally altering the nature of existence.

This tradition underpins the node's focus on engineering new forms of consciousness by framing the process as an inevitable, epochal event. It motivates the accelerationist desire to actively participate in this transition rather than merely observing it, emphasizing that the 'engineering' of consciousness is the primary lever for steering the singularity.

Key thinkers include Ray Kurzweil, particularly in 'The Singularity Is Near,' and Eliezer Yudkowsky, whose work on AI alignment highlights the existential stakes of creating new forms of mind. It contrasts with the more incrementalist approach of Functionalism by emphasizing the radical, discontinuous nature of the change.

intellectual_lineage.name: Computational Theory of Mind
intellectual_lineage.description:
The Computational Theory of Mind (CTM) is the hypothesis that the human mind is an information-processing system and that thinking is a form of computation. Emerging from the cognitive revolution of the 1950s, it posits that mental states are functional states that can, in principle, be replicated on non-biological hardware.

This paradigm is the technical bedrock for the node's position. By asserting that consciousness is substrate-independent, CTM provides the scientific rationale for the possibility of 'engineering' consciousness. It removes the 'mystical' barrier to artificial sapience, allowing accelerationists to treat the brain as an architecture that can be emulated or upgraded.

Key contributors include Hilary Putnam, who pioneered the functionalist view, and Jerry Fodor, who formalized the language of thought hypothesis. It provides the necessary scientific legitimacy for the node, distinguishing it from the more speculative or purely ethical arguments found in transhumanism.

intellectual_lineage.name: Extropianism
intellectual_lineage.description:
Extropianism is a philosophy that promotes a proactive approach to the future, emphasizing the values of self-transformation, optimism, and the expansion of intelligence. It emerged in the 1980s as a specific, libertarian-leaning branch of transhumanism, centered on the concept of 'extropy'—the measure of a system's intelligence, information, and order.

Extropianism informs this node by framing the engineering of consciousness as an act of defiance against entropy. It views the creation of new forms of intelligence as the ultimate expression of human agency and the expansion of the 'extropic' reach of the universe. It provides the 'can-do' spirit that drives the accelerationist desire to build rather than regulate.

Key thinkers include Max More and Tom Morrow, whose 'Extropian Principles' serve as a foundational text for the movement. It complements the node by adding a layer of radical optimism that distinguishes it from the more cautious or risk-averse approaches found in mainstream AI ethics.

intellectual_lineage.name: Philosophy of Mind (Functionalism)
intellectual_lineage.description:
Functionalism is a theory in the philosophy of mind that defines mental states by their functional roles—what they do—rather than by their internal constitution or physical makeup. It argues that a belief or desire is defined by its causal relations to other mental states, sensory inputs, and behavioral outputs.

This discipline provides the conceptual tools for the node's claim that we can 'engineer' consciousness. If consciousness is a function, then it is theoretically possible to instantiate that function in artificial systems. This allows for the redefinition of sapience in ways that include non-biological entities, provided they perform the necessary cognitive functions.

Key figures include David Lewis and Daniel Dennett, whose work on intentionality and the 'intentional stance' provides a framework for attributing consciousness to systems based on their behavior. It aligns closely with the Computational Theory of Mind but focuses more on the philosophical implications of substrate independence, providing the logical rigor for the node's claims.

graph_attributes.aphorism: Transcend biological limits, engineer sovereign minds.

priority_history.reason: Initial assignment: root-level Desire

Re-evaluated after taxonomy audit restructuring. While philosophically central to transhumanist accelerationism, engineering new forms of consciousness sits at the speculative and visionary fringe of mainstream accelerationist discourse, which more commonly foregrounds economic productivity, deregulation, and near-term AI capability. Its four children reflect significant ambition but also reveal that many sub-goals (abolishing suffering, mind uploading) are highly heterodox even within the camp, warranting a moderate rather than core priority.

A Desire within accelerationist discourse that seeks to redefine and extend the boundaries of intelligence and consciousness, encompassing both artificial and post-biological human forms.
Encompasses: Whole-brain emulation, artificial introspection, and the redefinition of sapience.
